notes.h: Carbohydrates: general formula and size groups
notes.b: Carbohydrates are the first of the four main biomolecules, the large carbon-based molecules of living things. They share one simple pattern in their formula and fall into three groups by size.
points: Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. Their general formula is Cx(H₂O)y, so hydrogen and oxygen are in the ratio 2 : 1, as in water. Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, is an example.
The name means “hydrated carbon” because of that ratio, but the molecule does not contain water molecules. The H and O atoms are simply bonded into the sugar in the same 2 : 1 proportion.
There are three groups by size: monosaccharides (one sugar unit), disaccharides (two units) and polysaccharides (many units).
Mono- and disaccharides are sugars: sweet, soluble in water and crystalline.
Polysaccharides are not sweet and are insoluble or only slightly soluble, which suits them to storage and structure, because a molecule that does not dissolve stays put inside a cell or in a wall.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name the elements in carbohydrates: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only. Give Cx(H₂O)y and the 2 : 1 ratio of hydrogen to oxygen if asked about the formula.

notes.b: Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates: a single sugar unit. They are the monomers (single building-block units) from which every other carbohydrate is made.
points: Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, is the main respiratory substrate (the molecule broken down in respiration to release energy) and the product of photosynthesis.
Fructose, the fruit sugar found in fruit and honey, has the same formula, C₆H₁₂O₆, but a different arrangement of atoms. Two molecules can share a formula and still be different sugars.
Galactose also has the formula C₆H₁₂O₆ and is a unit of lactose, the sugar in milk.
Glucose, fructose and galactose are all six-carbon sugars (hexoses).
Ribose and deoxyribose are five-carbon monosaccharides (pentoses). Ribose is found in RNA nucleotides and deoxyribose in DNA nucleotides. There is more on this in DNA, RNA and the Genetic Code.
Diagram: glucose drawn as a simple six-sided ring (hexagon) labelled glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆. Atom-by-atom structural formulas are not needed.
notes.tip: Don’t say fructose is C₅ or C₁₂: glucose, fructose and galactose all have the formula C₆H₁₂O₆. Learn one monosaccharide you can name for an examiner, such as glucose.

notes.b: Two monosaccharides can be joined to make a disaccharide. The way they join is the same reaction that later builds starch and other large molecules.
points: A disaccharide forms when two monosaccharides join by condensation, a reaction that releases one molecule of water. The link between the sugar units is a glycosidic bond.
Disaccharides have the formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, which is 2 × C₆H₁₂O₆ minus H₂O, because one water molecule is lost when the two units join.
Hydrolysis (splitting a bond by adding water) splits a disaccharide back into monosaccharides. It is the reverse of condensation.
Maltose (malt sugar) is glucose + glucose. It forms when starch is digested by amylase (an enzyme that breaks down starch) and is found in germinating grain.
Sucrose (table sugar, cane or beet sugar) is glucose + fructose. It is the form in which plants transport sugar in the phloem (the tissue that carries sugars around the plant).
Lactose (milk sugar) is glucose + galactose and is found in milk.
Diagram: two hexagons joined, with H₂O removed by condensation and returned by hydrolysis; label maltose = glucose + glucose.
notes.tip: Sucrose is glucose + fructose, not glucose + glucose, which is maltose. Lactose contains galactose. Questions ask for the units of named disaccharides, and the bond between sugar units is the glycosidic bond, not the peptide or ester bond.

notes.h: Polysaccharides: starch, glycogen, cellulose and chitin
notes.b: A polysaccharide is a very long chain of sugar units. Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all made of glucose, yet they do very different jobs because of how the units are linked and whether the chain branches.
points: A polysaccharide is a polymer (a long molecule made of many repeating units) of many monosaccharide units, often thousands, joined by condensation. Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all polymers of glucose; they differ in how the glucose units are linked and whether the chains branch.

Starch is the storage carbohydrate of plants, held as starch grains in cells of potato tubers, seeds and cereal grains. It is a mixture of amylose, an unbranched chain that coils into a helix, and amylopectin, a branched chain.
Being insoluble, starch does not draw water into cells by osmosis (water moving in towards a more concentrated solution), and its compact shape stores much glucose in a small space.

Glycogen is the storage carbohydrate of animals and fungi, stored mainly in the liver and muscles. It is more highly branched than amylopectin, so it has many chain ends from which glucose can be released quickly when energy is needed.

Cellulose is the structural carbohydrate of plants, forming the cell wall. Its glucose units are linked in a different orientation from starch, giving long, straight, unbranched chains that lie side by side. Many hydrogen bonds (weak attractions between neighbouring chains) hold them together, forming strong fibres.
Humans have no enzyme to digest cellulose, so it passes through the gut as dietary fibre (roughage). There is more on cellulose in Biomolecules and metabolism.
Chitin is a polysaccharide that contains nitrogen. It forms the cell walls of fungi and the exoskeletons (hard outer coverings) of insects and other arthropods.
Diagram: a chain of hexagons for starch (unbranched amylose and branched amylopectin), a more branched chain for glycogen, and parallel straight chains linked by cross-links for cellulose fibres.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for the storage polysaccharide in plants (starch) and in animals (glycogen), where glycogen is stored (liver and muscles), and a structural one (cellulose). Glycogen is not stored in plants, starch is not stored in animals, and cellulose is not a storage carbohydrate.

notes.b: Lipids are the second biomolecule group. The triglyceride, one of the main kinds, is built from just two kinds of smaller molecule joined by condensation.
points: Lipids are fats, oils and related compounds such as phospholipids. They contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with much less oxygen in proportion to carbon and hydrogen than carbohydrates, so they are not of the form Cx(H₂O)y. Phospholipids also contain phosphorus.
Lipids are insoluble in water but dissolve in organic solvents such as ethanol.
A triglyceride is one glycerol molecule joined to three fatty acids. Glycerol is a small molecule with three carbons, each carrying an –OH group, so it can bond to three fatty acids.
A fatty acid is a long hydrocarbon chain of carbon and hydrogen atoms with an acid (carboxyl, –COOH) group at one end.
Each fatty acid joins to glycerol by condensation, so forming one triglyceride releases three water molecules. The bond formed is an ester bond.
Hydrolysis by lipase (an enzyme that digests fats) reverses this, giving glycerol and fatty acids. There is more on this in The Digestive System.
Diagram: a triglyceride drawn as an E shape, with a vertical glycerol bar and three horizontal fatty acid tails, labelled glycerol, fatty acid and 3 H₂O removed.
notes.tip: A triglyceride is not a polymer, so don’t call fatty acids its monomers. Exams ask you to describe or draw one: glycerol plus three fatty acids, three waters released. The bond is an ester bond, not a glycosidic or peptide bond.

notes.b: Fats and oils have the same basic unit, the triglyceride. They differ in the fatty acids attached, and that decides whether they are solid or liquid at room temperature.
points: There are many different fatty acids, varying in chain length and in whether they contain carbon–carbon double bonds. Glycerol combines with different fatty acids to give many different fats and oils.
Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds, so the chain holds the maximum hydrogen. Their straight chains pack closely, so fats rich in them are solid at room temperature.
Saturated examples are butter, lard and the fat on meat. These are mostly animal fats.
Unsaturated fatty acids have one or more C=C double bonds, which put kinks (bends) in the chain. Kinked chains pack loosely, so oils are liquid at room temperature.
Unsaturated examples are olive oil, sunflower oil and fish oils. These are mostly from plants and fish.
notes.tip: To explain the difference between a fat and an oil, say that fats are solid and oils liquid at room temperature, and link this to saturated chains packing closely and kinked unsaturated chains packing loosely. They differ in melting point, not in their basic unit.

notes.b: A phospholipid is a triglyceride with one change: a phosphate group takes the place of a fatty acid. That small change gives the molecule one end that likes water and one that avoids it.
points: A phospholipid is glycerol joined to two fatty acids and a phosphate-containing group in place of the third fatty acid.
The phosphate head is hydrophilic (attracted to water). The two fatty acid tails are hydrophobic (repelled by water).
In water, phospholipids arrange themselves in a double layer (bilayer), with the heads facing the watery fluid on each side and the tails pointing inwards, away from the water.
This bilayer is the basis of every cell membrane. There is more on this in Transport Across Membranes and The Unit of Life — The Cell.
Diagram: a phospholipid drawn as a circle (head) with two wavy tails, labelled hydrophilic phosphate head and hydrophobic fatty acid tails; and a section of a bilayer.
notes.tip: When asked to describe or draw a phospholipid, give glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate group, and label the hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails. Remember that it has two fatty acids, whereas a triglyceride has three.

notes.b: Proteins are the third biomolecule group. Every protein is a chain built from the same 20 kinds of amino acid, joined by peptide bonds.
points: Proteins contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, and sometimes sulfur, phosphorus or other elements. Sulfur is in some amino acids such as cysteine and methionine, phosphorus is in casein (the main protein of milk), and iron is in haemoglobin. There is more on this in Minerals.
Proteins are made of amino acids. There are 20 different amino acids in the proteins of living things.

Each amino acid has a central carbon atom bonded to an amino group (–NH₂), an acid (carboxyl, –COOH) group, a hydrogen atom and a variable side group (R group). Only the R group differs between amino acids.
Humans cannot make some amino acids (essential amino acids), so these must be taken in from food.
Amino acids join by condensation between the –COOH group of one and the –NH₂ group of the next, releasing water. The bond formed is a peptide bond.
Two amino acids form a dipeptide; a short chain is a peptide; a long chain is a polypeptide. A protein is one or more polypeptides folded into a particular shape.
The sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide (its primary structure) is set by a gene. Because 20 amino acids can be arranged in any order and length, a vast number of different proteins is possible.
Diagram: the general structure of an amino acid, a central carbon with –NH₂, –COOH, –H and –R attached; and two amino acids joined by a peptide bond with H₂O released.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name the bond between amino acids (the peptide bond), the units of proteins (amino acids) and an element found in some proteins only (such as sulfur). Don’t confuse the peptide bond with the glycosidic bond (carbohydrates) or the ester bond (lipids).

notes.b: A polypeptide chain does not stay straight. It folds into a precise shape, and that shape is what lets a protein do its job. Damage the shape and the job is lost.
points: The chain coils into a helix or folds into a pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds (secondary structure). This folds further into a precise three-dimensional shape (tertiary structure), held by bonds between R groups, including sulfur bridges between cysteine units.
Some proteins consist of several polypeptides fitted together (quaternary structure). Haemoglobin has four polypeptide chains.
The shape determines the function, because other molecules must fit it. An enzyme’s active site or an antibody’s binding site fits only particular molecules.

Heat, extremes of pH and some chemicals break the bonds holding the shape, so the protein loses its shape and function. This is denaturation, usually permanent, e.g. egg white turns solid and white when cooked. There is more on this in Enzymes.
Fibrous proteins are long strands, insoluble and structural, such as keratin (hair, nails) and collagen (skin, tendons).
Globular proteins are folded into compact, roughly spherical shapes and are usually soluble, e.g. enzymes, antibodies, haemoglobin and insulin.
notes.tip: Exams ask why the shape of a protein matters and what denaturation is. Say that the shape fits particular molecules, that heat, extreme pH or chemicals break the bonds holding the shape, and that the protein then loses its function.

notes.b: Nucleic acids are the fourth biomolecule group. Like the other groups, they are built from repeating units, which are called nucleotides.
points: Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are polymers of nucleotides. Each nucleotide contains a sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base, so nucleic acids contain C, H, O, N and P. There is more on this in DNA, RNA and the Genetic Code.

notes.b: Putting the four groups side by side makes the differences easy to compare: which elements each contains, what its units are, which bond joins them and an example.
points: Carbohydrate: C, H, O; monosaccharides; glycosidic bond; glucose, sucrose, starch.
Lipid: C, H, O (plus P in phospholipids); glycerol and fatty acids; ester bond; triglycerides, phospholipids.
Protein: C, H, O, N (sometimes S, P or other elements); amino acids; peptide bond; enzymes, keratin.
Nucleic acid: C, H, O, N, P; nucleotides; DNA, RNA.
notes.tip: The three bonds are easily confused: glycosidic for carbohydrates, ester for lipids and peptide for proteins. Match each bond to its biomolecule when you answer.

keyTerms.definition: A single sugar unit, such as glucose, fructose or galactose; the monomer of carbohydrates.
Two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond, formed by condensation with loss of water.
A polymer of many monosaccharides, such as starch, glycogen, cellulose or chitin.
A lipid made of one glycerol and three fatty acids joined by ester bonds.
A lipid with two fatty acid tails and a phosphate head, which forms the bilayer of cell membranes.
The bond formed by condensation between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next.
The variable side group that distinguishes one amino acid from another.
The loss of a protein's shape, and so its function, when heat, extremes of pH or chemicals break the bonds holding it.

questions.prompt: Name the units that make up (i) a triglyceride and (ii) a protein, and name the bond that joins amino acids.
questions.model: (i) A triglyceride is made of one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids. (ii) A protein is made of amino acids. Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds, which form by condensation with the release of water.

questions.prompt: Compare the structures and functions of starch, glycogen and cellulose.
questions.model: All three are polymers of glucose. Starch is the storage carbohydrate of plants; it is a mixture of unbranched amylose, which coils into a helix, and branched amylopectin, and it is insoluble, so it stores much glucose compactly. Glycogen is the storage carbohydrate of animals and fungi, stored mainly in the liver and muscles; it is more highly branched than starch, so glucose can be released quickly from its many chain ends. Cellulose is the structural carbohydrate of plant cell walls; its long, unbranched chains lie side by side and are held by hydrogen bonds to form strong fibres.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a phospholipid and explain how this structure allows phospholipids to form cell membranes.
questions.model: A phospholipid has a glycerol backbone joined to two fatty acids and to a phosphate-containing group in place of the third fatty acid. The phosphate head is hydrophilic, so it is attracted to water, and the two fatty acid tails are hydrophobic, so they are repelled by water. In water, phospholipids arrange themselves in a double layer, a bilayer, with the heads facing the watery fluid on each side and the tails pointing inwards. This bilayer is the basis of cell membranes, because the arrangement follows directly from the hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails.
